"One open entry: D-0001 (blueprint R2, no cross-dependency; ADR 0002 is its argument). Reviewed against its exit condition and against the register's second test — whether its argument is still being carried on assertion.

EXIT CONDITION — NOT MET, and slice 2 does not move it. The condition is "a second consumer needs isolation: a different shape of the same structure, or a group that must not see part of it. The generator then gains per-group projections over the same bridge." Slice 2's logistics manager wants the same bridge in the same shape and is not forbidden anything the sales director sees. The stated cost — "the first thing to break is a slice needing a measure defined one way for one reader and another way for another" — has not been incurred either: FREIGHT_ORDERS_AMOUNT means one thing to both readers. The entry stays open, and its status column stays 'open'.

BUT ITS REVIEW TRIGGER FIRES. The register's own Review section says an entry "should also be re-read the moment a second consumer appears, not only when isolation is demanded, because by then the shared structure will already have shaped both readers." Slice 2 is that moment: it is the first slice with a second question and therefore, per ADR 0005 ("one question, one slice, one branch, one page") and `.claude/skills/destination/SKILL.md` ("one app, a page per question"), the first with a second reader of `dar__uss`. This is the review the register asked for, and it should be recorded rather than passed over silently.

WHAT ONE n:1 EDGE DEMONSTRATES. D-0001's 'Why' rests on two clauses: (a) "keys inherit along many-to-one relationships" and (b) "measures stay on the stage that owns them", together making the shared structure "additive by construction". Slice 2 discharges (a) and half of (b), and does not touch the other half.

Demonstrated for the first time: that a key can be carried along an n:1 edge onto the many side, and that summing the many side's measure grouped by the one side's attribute is not multiplied. Concretely, ORDER is the many side, CUSTOMER the one side; there is exactly one bridge row per placed order however many orders a customer has, so `sum(_measure__order__freight_orders_amount)` grouped by `customer.customer_country` totals to the same grand total as ungrouped. That is checkable against the real warehouse and slice 2 should add the check. It is a genuine discharge: the walk now has one edge instead of zero, and ADR 0002's "a zero-edge walk is a valid walk" stops being the only case the code has ever run.

NOT demonstrated, and this is the half the fan trap is named for: a measure owned by the ONE side, summed at a grain where that side appears many times. Slice 2 adds no CUSTOMER event and no CUSTOMER measure, so there is nothing on the parent side that could multiply. ADR 0002's own Confirmation section describes the missing test exactly — "a fixture with two parents and three children, where sum(_measure__parent__…) must still be the parent total and not three times it" — and says it "needs two grains… It lands with the second grain". Slice 2 adds a second ENTITY but still only one grain in the bridge: one stage, order/placed. `docs/questions/README.md` agrees and dates it: "Slice 4 is where the shared-bridge deviation (D-0001) stops being carried on assertion — a second grain is the first thing a measure could multiply across", and slice 4's line reads "the fan-out proof: freight sits on the order and must not multiply across its lines." So slice 2 creates the very measure whose non-multiplication is slice 4's proof, one slice before the thing it must not multiply across exists.

One correction to that dating, in slice 2's favour. ADR 0002 says the fan-out test "cannot be yet" because "this slice has one entity" — but the machinery tests use neutral fixtures held as data files (§6, ADR 0001), not the business model, so the true blocker in slice 1 was that the generator had no relationship support at all, not that the business had one entity. The moment slice 2 teaches the generator to walk an edge, the machinery half of the fan-out test becomes writable: extend `tests/fixtures/dab/model.yaml` with a neutral CHILD entity, a neutral n:1 edge and a measure on PARENT, and assert that the child branch of the union emits a typed NULL in the parent's measure column and that the parent's key is inherited onto the child stage. Slice 2 should write it. What still waits for slice 4 is the *data* half — the same property proved against the real warehouse with real rows, which is what "stops being carried on assertion" properly means.

RECOMMENDATION. Keep D-0001 open and leave its four fields unedited — the reasons that made it necessary have not changed. Do three things instead: (1) update the Review paragraph in `docs/deviations.md`, whose current sentence names slice 1 by hand ("which slice 1's single entity does not exercise at all") and will be stale the moment slice 2 lands — replace it with what is now exercised (the walk, key inheritance, additivity of a child-side measure across a parent-side dimension) and what is not (a parent-side measure at a child grain, which is slice 4); (2) write the neutral-fixture fan-out machinery test in slice 2, since it is now writable, so slice 4 inherits only the data half; (3) record in slice 2's ADR that the second consumer has appeared without demanding isolation, because the register asked for that re-read explicitly and an unrecorded review is indistinguishable from one that never happened.

One footnote on attribution: the blog (*the-consumption-layer-generates-itself*) describes the walk as inheriting "the keys and measures of everything you reach", while ADR 0002 says keys inherit and measures do not. These agree in practice — in a USS the measure *column* exists on every stage and is non-null only on the owning one, which is exactly what `_branch` emits — but the ADR's prose reads as a departure from the blog it cites. Worth a clarifying sentence when 0002 is next touched, not a change of behaviour."
input.theJoinOnPaper:
"WHICH STAGE OWNS THE MEASURE. The `order` stage, on the `placed` event. Freight is a NUMBER on ORDER (one charge per order), and `src/adss/uss.py` requires a sum measure to name an attribute of the event's own entity — `_stage_cte` emits `cast(placed."FREIGHT" AS DECIMAL(28, 8)) AS _measure__order__freight_orders_amount` reading `dab."view_ORDER_hist"`. There is no alternative: CUSTOMER has no freight attribute, and a CUSTOMER stage carrying freight would be the fan trap written down as a design. Slice 2 therefore adds no stage — the bridge still has exactly one branch, one row per order whose PLACED_ON is set, and gains one measure column appended after `_measure__order__placed_orders_count`.

WHICH KEY IS INHERITED. `customer_key`, onto the `order` stage, along ORDER_IS_PLACED_BY_CUSTOMER — many orders, one customer, so the edge is many-to-one and the walk may cross it (blog *the-consumption-layer-generates-itself*: "follow any path that never fans out, and inherit everything along it"). Never the reverse: `order_key` must not propagate to a customer stage, and there is no customer stage in slice 2 anyway. The bridge's key columns become (`order_key`, `customer_key`) in that order — model order, which means CUSTOMER must be APPENDED after ORDER in `dab/model.yaml` or the published contract is rearranged rather than extended (ADR 0002, blueprint B7).

Two code facts make this more than a declaration. `entity_keys()` currently scopes key columns to entities that own an event, and `_generate()` scopes peripherals the same way; CUSTOMER owns no event, so as the code stands there would be neither a `customer_key` column nor a `dar__uss.customer` table. Both must become walk-scoped before any of the rest is possible.

THE GENERATOR'S OWN JOIN — the decision below the documented rule. The `placed` CTE must acquire `CUSTOMER_key` from the relationship object. Two properties are required and neither is written down anywhere: (1) the join is LEFT, or an order with no customer disappears from the bridge and its freight leaves the grand total silently; (2) the relationship object must be reduced to one row per ORDER_key — latest `eff_tmstp` — before the join, or the stage multiplies and `sum(freight)` doubles. The pair carries `eff_tmstp` and `ver_tmstp` (spike 2 finding 4), so more than one row per order is a live possibility the moment a customer id changes across two loads. ADR 0002's fan-trap argument is about measures being copied down an edge; it does not cover a key-inheritance join that fans out, which produces the same wrong number by a different route.

THE ANSWER QUERY. Three references, and the joins are decided one at a time:

  FROM dar__uss._bridge AS b
  INNER JOIN dar__uss._calendar AS cal ON b._event_date = cal.date_key
  LEFT JOIN dar__uss.customer AS c ON b.customer_key = c.customer_key
  WHERE b._event = 'placed'
  GROUP BY cal.quarter_label, c.customer_country
  ORDER BY order_quarter, customer_country

`_calendar` — INNER. `_event_date` is the row's own date, non-null by the column contract, and the calendar is generated dense and daily from `min(_event_date)` to `max(_event_date)` over the bridge itself, so every event date has a calendar row by construction. Note this join is on a date, not a key: ADR 0002's INNER/LEFT rule is about keys and does not literally cover it; INNER is right here for the reason just given, not by appeal to that rule.

`customer` — LEFT, and this is the rule going live. `customer_key` is INHERITED on the `order` stage, not the stage's own key, so ADR 0002 and the dar skill both require LEFT. An INNER join would drop every order whose customer key is null and shrink the freight total — the exact "routing a number through the layers changed it" failure the acceptance check exists to catch, arriving through the query rather than the pipeline.

`dar__uss."order"` — not joined at all. The question needs no ORDER attribute: freight is a measure on the bridge, the quarter comes from the calendar, the country comes from CUSTOMER. If a later question needs one, that join is INNER, because `order_key` is the row's own stage key.

WHAT THE LEFT JOIN COSTS AND WHY IT IS STILL RIGHT. In the recording it costs nothing and buys nothing: all 830 order records carry a non-null CustomerId across 89 distinct values, so LEFT and INNER return identical rows and the acceptance check cannot tell them apart. That is the uncomfortable part — slice 2's headline rule is unenforced by slice 2's own data. Three things fix it: a machinery test over a neutral fixture with a dangling child that asserts the generated stage CTE uses a LEFT join; a data check comparing `sum(_measure__order__freight_orders_amount)` over the whole bridge against `sum(freight)` over `das__staged.orders__current WHERE order_date IS NOT NULL`, which catches both a dropped row and a multiplied one independent of any grouping; and a check that the count of bridge rows with a null `customer_key` equals the count of orders whose customer is absent from `customers__current`.

THE CONTROL QUERY MUST MIRROR IT, ONE JOIN AT A TIME.

  FROM das__staged.orders__current AS o
  LEFT JOIN das__staged.customers__current AS c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
  WHERE o.order_date IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY strftime(o.order_date, '%Y') || '-Q' || cast(quarter(o.order_date) AS VARCHAR), c.country

LEFT, for the same reason and stated as the same reason — slice 1's question file set the precedent of writing down that both queries take the same position deliberately rather than by coincidence. `WHERE o.order_date IS NOT NULL` mirrors the stage's own `WHERE placed."PLACED_ON" IS NOT NULL`; without it the control counts freight the bridge cannot hold, and this matters more for a sum than it did for slice 1's count, because a reader may reconcile the total against the source's total freight. The quarter label must be composed to match `_calendar.quarter_label` exactly ('1996-Q3'), which is `strftime('%Y') || '-Q' || quarter()` in the generator.

THE TWO EDGE CASES, AND WHETHER THE QUESTION HAS TO SAY.

An order with no customer — null CustomerId, or a CustomerId absent from the Customers recording. Bridge row exists, freight present, `customer_key` null; LEFT join yields a null country; the freight lands in a null-country group in BOTH queries and they agree. The generator never invents a member (§1.3), so there is no 'Unknown' row and no `coalesce`. THE QUESTION HAS TO SAY — §1.3 puts the choice in the question file explicitly, and slice 1's `## Nulls` section is the precedent. Neither case occurs in the orders recording (zero null CustomerIds in 830 records), and whether any of the 89 customer ids is absent from Customers cannot be known until `adss das record --contract customers` has run — so the question must state the position, and the slice must actually check the dangling case rather than assume it away.

A customer with no orders. Peripheral row exists; no bridge row anywhere, because there is no customer stage and no order points at them. The query drives from `_bridge`, so that customer never appears — and neither does their country, unless another customer in it ordered. Both queries behave identically, so the check stays green. This is correct for the question as asked: no order means no freight, and a zero row would require a RIGHT or FULL join the architecture does not offer and the question does not ask for. NO RULE REQUIRES THE QUESTION TO SAY — this is a consequence of the grain, not a null-handling choice. But one sentence is worth writing anyway, because "why is Poland missing?" is the first thing the logistics manager will ask, and the honest answer is that no customer there has ever ordered."
gaps: The columns of the relationship pair object are unrecorded. Spike 2 counted `ORDER_CUSTOMER_x` at 3 rows and listed it as a BASE TABLE, but never ran DESCRIBE on it and never selected from it. `DESCRIBE dab.view_ORDER_IS_PLACED_BY_CUSTOMER` was captured (ORDER_key, CUSTOMER_key, type_key, eff_tmstp, ver_tmstp); the `_x` table's shape was not, and the daana documentation in the blog folder never describes it either. ADR 0002 instructs the generator to read this object, so the record depends on a shape nobody has looked at.

ADR 0002's reason for rejecting the relationship VIEW is not backed by any spike observation. The record says those views "rank pairs by effective timestamp and keep the open rows, [so] a changed foreign key can drop out of the view entirely". No spike captured the view's SQL definition, and no spike changed a foreign key across two loads. This is the argument that decides which DAB object the generator reads, and it is currently reasoned rather than observed.

No relationship has ever been observed loading under the configuration this repository mandates. Spike 2's ORDER mapping used `ingestion_strategy: TRANSACTIONAL` with `batch_expression: ingested_at` and `entity_effective_timestamp_expression: order_date` — both forbidden here by M3 and M4. So the only evidence that `ORDER_CUSTOMER_x` is populated at all comes from a configuration conventions §1.4 refuses. Whether the pair object is produced correctly under `FULL_LOG` + `extracted_at` is untested by anything.

What the engine does with a null or dangling foreign key is unknown. Does `target_transformation_expression: customer_id` evaluating to NULL produce no pair row, or a pair row with a null CUSTOMER_key? Does a customer id that exists on the order but in no customer record produce a pair row pointing at a CUSTOMER_key that has no `_desc` rows? Neither was exercised — spike 2's three orders all had valid customers. Both cases change what the bridge holds.

Whether daana's model-level relationship block accepts an `id` key is unknown. The documented shape (blog `doc-ch1.txt`) is `name: IS_PLACED_BY` with `source_entity_id` and `target_entity_id` and no `id`, but conventions §1.2 requires that "entity, attribute and relationship identifiers are UPPER_SNAKE_CASE, with `id` and `name` holding the identical string". If the schema has no `id` key for a relationship, that clause cannot be satisfied and needs clarifying; if it does, nothing has confirmed it.

Nothing establishes how many customers Northwind has or whether any has no orders. 89 distinct CustomerIds appear across the 830 recorded orders; the Customers recording does not exist yet. Whether the 89 are a strict subset of the customers, and whether any recorded customer id on an order is absent from Customers, are both determinable only after `adss das record --contract customers` runs — and both change what the question's null section has to say.

No rule exists for the generator's own inheritance join. Conventions and ADR 0002 state the INNER/LEFT rule for the *reader's* query only. That the stage's join to the relationship object must be LEFT, and must be reduced to one row per source key before joining, is nowhere written — and both failures are silent (a shrunk total, a doubled total).

No rule forbids an answer query joining one peripheral to another. `check_question` only checks which schemas are named, so slice 2 could be faked entirely — model an ORDER foreign-key attribute, join `dar__uss."order"` to `dar__uss.customer` on it, and never touch the inherited key — while every test and check stays green.

No rule says how a NUMBER attribute in `model.yaml` is named relative to the §2 measure that sums it, nor how their two definitions divide the labour. §2 governs measure ids in `uss.yaml`; §1.2 governs attribute ids in `model.yaml`; nothing connects them, and the first sum makes them adjacent.

No rule says what `effective_timestamp:` should be for a new attribute. `src/adss/model.py` does not read the key at all — it is engine-only configuration — and neither conventions nor the dab skill mentions it, yet slice 2 adds several attributes and will pick values for all of them silently. The existing model has `false` on ORDER_NUMBER, `true` on DESTINATION_COUNTRY, and nothing on the START_TIMESTAMP; the neutral fixture uses `true` for its NUMBER attribute.

Nothing says where the DOUBLE cast for charting belongs. The destination skill says to cast aggregates to DOUBLE; ADR 0005 says the page runs `uss.sql` verbatim; `checks.py` compares result tuples with `==`. Put the cast in the query and the first sum measure fails the acceptance check on float-versus-Decimal comparison, with numbers that print identically.

Nothing says what `answer.png` is when one app renders two questions. `docs/questions/01-.../answer.png` is byte-identical to `.screenshots/app.png`, `Project.destination` is a single hardcoded file, and `shoot()` writes one image at a fixed 1800px height. A second question makes the page taller (truncation risk) and makes one screenshot the record for two questions — while ADR 0005 says the picture records what *that* question was accepted on. Whether q01's accepted image is left alone (it should be) and how q02's is produced are both undecided.

The measure has no currency and nothing says what to do about it. Northwind's Freight carries no currency property, and the engine's type vocabulary has a `UNIT` type for exactly this (daana's own example pairs `order_value_amount` with `order_value_currency`). S1 forbids inventing one in DAS. So the honest move is a definition that records the absence — but no rule says a money measure must state its currency or say that the source does not, and §2's unit slot (`amount`) does not carry it.

binds.rule: F3 — DAB reads only DAS; and M1 — `table:` names a `das__staged` object and nothing else

The relationship is declared, not hand-joined: the ORDER→CUSTOMER edge is expressed as a `relationships:` entry in the order mapping (`id`, `source_table`, `target_transformation_expression`), which is the shape daana documents (blog `doc-ch1.txt` lines 296-302). Writing the customer country onto ORDER by any expression that reads the customers table is forbidden twice over — by M1 and by M5.

binds.rule: F2 — DAR reads only DAB; F1 — analytical usage reads only DAR
binds.whatItForbidsHere: `uss.sql` for question 02 may not mention `das__`, `dab.`, `dab__` or `read_parquet`; `staged.sql` may not mention `dab` or `dar__uss`. The marimo page runs `uss.sql` verbatim, so a reach past DAR would render, pass, and be exactly the invisible dependency F1 exists to prevent.

binds.rule: B7 — change is additive: a new attribute, entity or relationship is a new structure, never a modification
binds.source: docs/blueprint.md (DAB B7); ADR 0002 "new entities and measures are appended, never inserted or renamed"
binds.whatItForbidsHere: Concretely, this forbids putting CUSTOMER *before* ORDER in `dab/model.yaml`. `entity_keys()` orders the bridge's key columns by model order (`src/adss/uss.py`), so an inserted entity would rearrange the published column contract rather than extend it. CUSTOMER is appended after ORDER; FREIGHT is appended after DESTINATION_COUNTRY inside ORDER; the freight measure is appended after PLACED_ORDERS_COUNT inside the PLACED event. Nothing existing is renamed, retyped or reordered.

binds.rule: B8 — meaning is defined exactly once, in `dab/model.yaml`; every entity, attribute and relationship has a `definition`
binds.whatItForbidsHere: CUSTOMER, its country attribute, ORDER's freight attribute and the relationship each need one definition written for a person, and the question file may only reference them by token (`{{...}}`). It forbids `question.md` paraphrasing what freight is; forbids the DAS contract's `description` saying what freight means to the business (§1.1 keeps it to "Edm.Decimal, Scale=Variable"); and forbids the destination writing its own gloss — `destinations/app.py` copies `definitions()` verbatim.

binds.rule: B5 — atomic; B6 — reusable; B3/B4 — time-variant and non-volatile
binds.whatItForbidsHere: Forbids a pre-aggregated freight-per-country structure anywhere in DAB, and forbids a CUSTOMER attribute shaped by this one question (a country *grouping*, a 'region bucket'). B3/B4 mean the CUSTOMER mapping historizes rather than snapshots — which M3 and M4 then make physical.

binds.rule: M3 — `ingestion_strategy: FULL_LOG`; M4 — `entity_effective_timestamp_expression: extracted_at`
binds.source: docs/conventions.md §1.4 M3, M4; ADR 0004; spike 2 findings 7, 8, 9
binds.whatItForbidsHere: The customers mapping may not use `FULL`. M4 forbids dating a CUSTOMER version by anything but `extracted_at` — and Northwind's Customer entity has no date property at all, so there is nothing else to be tempted by.

binds.rule: M6 — a relationship's `id` is `<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>`; its `source_table` is byte-identical to its group's `table`; its target expression mirrors the target entity's own key expression exactly
binds.source: docs/conventions.md §1.4 M6 — LIVE FOR THE FIRST TIME in slice 2
binds.whatItForbidsHere: Three concrete refusals. (1) The id must be `ORDER_IS_PLACED_BY_CUSTOMER`, not `IS_PLACED_BY` and not `ORDER_CUSTOMER`. (3) `target_transformation_expression:` must be spelled exactly as `customer-mapping.yaml`'s own key expression — if CUSTOMER's `primary_keys: [customer_id]` is a bare column, the relationship's target expression is the bare `customer_id`; if it is wrapped in `cast(... AS VARCHAR)`, the relationship's must be too. A differently spelled key produces pairs that join to nothing. `src/adss/mapping.py:check_mapping` does not check M6 and `read_mapping` does not even parse the `relationships:` key, so all three are currently unenforced.

binds.rule: M2 — exactly one `primary_keys` entry; M5 — an attribute expression reads its own row; M7 — every mapped table carries at least one attribute
binds.whatItForbidsHere: `customer-mapping.yaml` gets one primary key (`customer_id`), never two — two entries are two *alternate identifiers* to the engine and cannot be undone once loaded. tensions.rule: ADR 0002: "The generator reads `view_<entity>_hist` and the relationship pair objects, and nothing else" — versus ADR 0004: "DAR reads the `view_*` layer only. Not `_focal`, not `_idfr`, not `_with_rel`."
tensions.howSliceTwoStrainsIt: These two records contradict each other and slice 2 is the first slice in which the contradiction has an object to be about. `ORDER_CUSTOMER_x` is a BASE TABLE, not a `view_*` object (spike 2 finding 2 lists it under BASE TABLE alongside `ORDER_desc`). ADR 0002 says read it and explicitly rejects the alternative: "Reading the relationship *views* rather than the pair objects is the subtle one: those views rank pairs by effective timestamp and keep the open rows, and our effective timestamp is the moment DAS observed the row, so a changed foreign key can drop out of the view entirely." ADR 0004 says the opposite, in the record that is meant to be the home for facts about this engine on this platform. `.claude/skills/dab/SKILL.md` reproduces both positions in adjacent bullets ("DAR reads the `view_*` layer only" and "Relationship keys come from `view_<src>_<rel>_<tgt>` or the pair table"). Worse: no spike observed `ORDER_CUSTOMER_x`'s columns, and no spike observed the SQL behind `view_ORDER_IS_PLACED_BY_CUSTOMER` — so ADR 0002's stated reason for rejecting the view is not grounded in anything recorded in spike-findings.json. Whichever object is chosen, the choice is currently being made on an unverified claim.
tensions.resolution: Recourse 3 — change the rule, by superseding. Recommend: slice 2's ADR (0006) settles which DAB object the generator reads for an inherited key, on evidence gathered first (DESCRIBE both objects, and observe what each does when a foreign key changes across two loads), and supersedes ADR 0004's sentence "DAR reads the `view_*` layer only" with the narrower true statement. Recourse 1 is not enough — this is not an ambiguity, it is two records giving opposite instructions — and the §8 exception that allows a record to be corrected in place has closed, because both were written in slice 1.

tensions.rule: ADR 0002's column contract: "`<entity>_key` … one per entity in model order"; and `dar__uss.<entity>` is a peripheral table, one per entity
tensions.howSliceTwoStrainsIt: The implementation is narrower than the contract, and slice 2 is where the gap bites. `src/adss/uss.py:entity_keys` computes `touched = {event.entity_id for event in uss.events}` and emits a key column only for entities that own an event. `src/adss/cli.py:_generate` builds peripherals from the same set. CUSTOMER has no event in slice 2 — no customer stage, no customer measure — so as the code stands the generator would emit no `customer_key` column and no `dar__uss.customer` table, and the question would be unanswerable. Neither existing check can see this: `test_the_bridge_column_contract_is_an_order_not_a_set` and `checks.py`'s DESCRIBE comparison both derive what they expect from `bridge_columns()`, the same function that is wrong. `entity_keys`'s own docstring admits the shape of this blind spot for the sibling case of ordering.
tensions.resolution: None of the three recourses applies cleanly — the rule fits and the code does not, so this is a defect, not a rule question. But there is a small rule question inside it that should be settled at the same time by recourse 1 (clarify this page / the ADR): does an entity in the model that no stage can reach get a key column? ADR 0002 read literally says yes ("one per entity"); the USS walk says no (blog *consumption-layer-generates-itself*: "follow any path that never fans out, and inherit everything along it"). Recommend: state the contract as "one key column per entity reachable from any staged entity by the many-to-one walk, in model order — the walk's fixed point, not the event list", fix `entity_keys` and `_generate` to that, and add a machinery test over a neutral two-entity fixture whose expectation is written out by hand rather than derived from `bridge_columns()`.

tensions.rule: §1.2: "No source name appears anywhere in `dab/model.yaml` — not in an id, not in a name, not in a definition, not in a description" (hard rule)
tensions.howSliceTwoStrainsIt: Northwind's Customer entity has a `Country` property and its Order entity has a `Freight` property (verified in the OData metadata). Slice 2 needs a country attribute on CUSTOMER and a NUMBER attribute on ORDER for the sum to read. Under the rule's literal text, `CUSTOMER_COUNTRY` and `FREIGHT` both contain a string that is a source column name — `country` and `freight` will both appear as `target_name`s in `das/contracts/*.yaml`. Slice 1 dodged this entirely: `ORDER_NUMBER`, `PLACED_ON` and `DESTINATION_COUNTRY` share no substring with `order_id`, `order_date` or `ship_country`. The document also undercuts its own rule two lines earlier: §1.2's singular-names row illustrates itself with `SHIP_COUNTRY`, which is precisely the mechanical snake_case of Northwind's `ShipCountry` and precisely the name slice 1 refused to use. Note that this bites only `model.yaml`: §1.2's own arbiter sentence says `dab/uss.yaml` is governed by §1.3 and §2, so the measure id `FREIGHT_ORDERS_AMOUNT` is not in scope — only the attribute it sums is.
tensions.resolution: Recourse 1 — clarify this page. The rule was aimed at moving a dependency, not at forbidding a word the domain owns; the operative test is whether the name is the *source's coinage for the thing*. `ShipCountry` is Northwind's coinage for a concept the business calls the destination, so renaming it was right. `Country` and `Freight` are the domain's own words that Northwind also happens to use, so keeping them moves no dependency: replace Northwind and the business still calls it the customer's country and the freight it paid. Recommend: add that sentence and a worked example to §1.2, replace the stale `SHIP_COUNTRY` illustration with one that is not a source name, and name the attributes `CUSTOMER_COUNTRY` and `FREIGHT`. Do not invent `BASED_IN_COUNTRY` to dodge the string match — an invented name that exists only to evade a rule is the quiet exception §11 refuses, and it hides the rule question instead of settling it.

tensions.rule: §1.2 guideline: "Descriptive attributes are prefixed with their entity (`CUSTOMER_NAME`, `ORDER_LINE_ID`) … The prefix is what makes an attribute readable once it has been inherited into a wide DAR row"; against §1.3 hard rule: "Attribute columns are the lower-cased attribute identifier, unchanged"
tensions.howSliceTwoStrainsIt: Following the guideline gives `CUSTOMER_COUNTRY`, and §1.3 then forces the DAR column to be `dar__uss.customer.customer_country` — a stutter that will be read a hundred times and cannot be shortened. Meanwhile the guideline's stated *reason* does not hold in this architecture: ADR 0002 decided that only keys inherit, so there is no wide DAR row carrying another entity's attributes. Attributes live on per-entity peripherals, where the table name already qualifies them. So the guideline is buying readability against a row shape this system does not build. Cutting the other way: this slice's entire point is that the customer's country and the order's destination country are different countries, and a flat glossary listing `COUNTRY` next to `DESTINATION_COUNTRY` invites exactly the confusion the question exists to expose.
tensions.resolution: Recourse 1 — clarify this page. Recommend keeping the prefix (`CUSTOMER_COUNTRY`) and accepting `customer.customer_country`, but rewriting the guideline's *why*, which is currently false here: the prefix earns its keep because attribute identifiers are read in one flat glossary and one flat `defines:` list, not because DAR rows are wide. A guideline whose stated reason does not apply is one a reviewer cannot use to tell a real violation from a case it was never aimed at, which is what §How-to-read-a-rule says the why is for.

tensions.rule: B8 — "Meaning is defined exactly once"; §1.2 — every attribute has a definition; `src/adss/uss.py:read_uss` — every measure has a definition
tensions.howSliceTwoStrainsIt: The first sum measure forces two definitions of one number. `ORDER.FREIGHT` needs a definition in `model.yaml`, and `ORDER.measures.FREIGHT_ORDERS_AMOUNT` needs one in `uss.yaml`, and both are about the same money. Slice 1 never met this because a count measure sums nothing — `PLACED_ORDERS_COUNT` has no attribute behind it, so its definition had no rival. The failure mode is the one B8 names: the two drift, and the glossary on the page shows one while the bridge computes from the other. Nothing in conventions §1.2 or §2 says how the labour divides.
tensions.resolution: Recourse 1 — clarify this page. Recommend adding to §2: the attribute's definition says what the number *is* on one instance ("the charge the business paid the carrier to deliver this order; the source states no currency"); the measure's definition says what *aggregating* it means and over what set ("freight across orders, on the day each order was placed; additive along every dimension the order reaches"). If the measure's definition can be written without repeating the attribute's, they are not two definitions of one thing. Add the split as a worked example beside `revenue_order_lines_amount`, which has the same shape and is already in the table.

tensions.rule: §10: "The staged query reads `das__staged.<table>__current`"; and ADR 0005: "the control query has a shelf life … from the first question spanning two sources … Slice 6 is where that bill arrives"
tensions.howSliceTwoStrainsIt: Slice 2's control must join `das__staged.orders__current` to `das__staged.customers__current` on `customer_id`. §10 says `<table>` in the singular and nothing in `check_question` counts tables, so a two-table control passes mechanically — but the convention's text does not say whether it is permitted. And the control now encodes the same decision the DAB relationship encodes: "an order's customer is the one whose CustomerId matches". Independence weakens by exactly that much. ADR 0005's *dating* survives: `docs/questions/README.md` calls slice 6 "**The second source.** A file drop with its own customer identifiers", so "two sources" means two source systems and slice 2 spans two entity sets of one. But ADR 0005's *reason* — "reimplementing DAB inside the check" — starts being paid here, one join early, and the record does not say so.
tensions.resolution: Recourse 1 — clarify this page. Recommend: §10 gains a sentence saying the control may read more than one `__current` view and may join them on the source's own declared referential constraint, because that is still the source's vocabulary and not DAB's; and that the moment the control needs identity *resolution* rather than a declared foreign key, it has stopped being independent and the arrangement is over. Slice 2's ADR should record honestly that the shelf life started running one slice earlier than ADR 0005 predicted, and what remains of the check's value: it still catches a dropped row, a multiplied measure and a mis-inherited key, which are precisely slice 2's three risks.

tensions.rule: §10 / ADR 0005 — the answer query reads `dar__uss` and nothing else; ADR 0002 — keys inherit along many-to-one relationships
tensions.howSliceTwoStrainsIt: Nothing forbids `uss.sql` joining two peripherals to each other. If the model gave ORDER a `CUSTOMER_NUMBER` attribute, the answer query could read `_bridge` → `dar__uss."order"` (INNER, own key) → `dar__uss.customer` on `o.customer_number = c.customer_number`, never touch `customer_key`, and pass every existing check: `check_question` only looks for forbidden schema prefixes. The relationship would be modelled, deployed and inherited, and the slice would demonstrate none of it. This is the invisible way to fake slice 2, and it is one attribute away.
tensions.resolution: Recourse 1 — clarify this page. Recommend a new hard rule in §10 or §1.3: an answer query joins each peripheral to the bridge on that entity's key column, never a peripheral to another peripheral; and a foreign key is never modelled as an attribute of the referring entity, because that is a second expression of a relationship the model already declares (M5's why already says every join must come from a declared relationship, but says it only about mapping expressions). Both halves are cheaply checkable in `check_question`.

tensions.rule: `.claude/skills/destination/SKILL.md`: "Cast an aggregate to `DOUBLE` before charting: DuckDB `DECIMAL` reaches the frontend as a decimal type the chart library cannot encode" — against ADR 0005: "the page reads the question's own `uss.sql`" and `src/adss/checks.py`: `control == answer` on Python tuples
tensions.howSliceTwoStrainsIt: Slice 1's measure is a count and `uss.sql` casts it to `BIGINT`, so this never arose. The first sum returns `DECIMAL(38, 8)` from the star schema and `DECIMAL(38, 4)` from the source; `Decimal` comparison is by value, so those agree. But if the DOUBLE cast is put inside `uss.sql` to satisfy the chart, the acceptance check compares a `float` against a `Decimal`, and in Python `Decimal('32.38') == 32.38` is False for most values — the question would go red with a difference nobody can see in the numbers as printed.
tensions.resolution: Recourse 1 — clarify this page. Recommend: §10 or the destination skill states that the cast for charting happens in the page, over the returned frame, never in `uss.sql` — because `uss.sql` is run verbatim by both the page and the check, and a presentation concern in it changes what the check compares. Keep `uss.sql` returning DECIMAL; cast in `destinations/app.py` on the polars frame.

tensions.rule: §1.4 M6 — "its target expression mirrors the target entity's own key expression exactly"; and `src/adss/mapping.py:check_mapping(mapping)`, which sees one mapping at a time
tensions.howSliceTwoStrainsIt: M6's third clause is a constraint between two files: the relationship's `target_transformation_expression` in `order-mapping.yaml` must mirror `customer-mapping.yaml`'s `primary_keys[0]`. `check_mapping` takes a single `Mapping` and cannot express it, and `read_mapping` does not parse `relationships:` at all. Separately, "exactly" reads as byte-identical text, but the two expressions are evaluated against *different tables* — here they coincide only because Northwind spells the foreign key `CustomerId` on Orders and the key `CustomerId` on Customers, so both become `customer_id`. A future slice whose foreign key has a different column name makes the literal reading impossible to satisfy.
tensions.resolution: Recourse 1 — clarify this page. Recommend: restate M6's third clause as "the same transformation, applied to the referring table's own foreign-key column" — the shape must match (bare column against bare column, `cast(... AS VARCHAR)` against `cast(... AS VARCHAR)`), the column name need not — and note that the `source_table` clause remains byte-identical because that one really is the same string. Then give the checker the whole set of mappings so it can enforce it, and land the failing test in the same commit.

tensions.rule: ADR 0002: "a `sum()` over the bridge is right without the reader knowing how the model is shaped"; the fan-trap argument behind D-0001
tensions.howSliceTwoStrainsIt: The fan trap ADR 0002 argues about is a *measure* being copied down an edge. Slice 2 creates a second one it does not discuss: the generator's own join. The `order` stage CTE must acquire `CUSTOMER_key` from the pair object, and if that object holds more than one row per order — which it will the moment an order's customer changes across two loads, since the pair carries `eff_tmstp` (spike 2 finding 4) — the stage multiplies, and `sum(_measure__order__freight_orders_amount)` doubles with no error. The same join, done as INNER instead of LEFT, silently *drops* every order with no customer and shrinks the total. Both failures are in the generator, one level below the rule that is written down (which is about the reader's query), and no rule covers either.
tensions.resolution: Recourse 1 — clarify this page, once slice 2's ADR has decided it. Recommend the generator-side rule be stated in §1.3 alongside the reader-side one: the stage's join to a relationship object is LEFT and must be proved one-to-at-most-one — the object is reduced to one row per source key by latest `eff_tmstp` before it is joined — because an inheritance join that fans out multiplies the owning stage's measure exactly as copying it would. The good news is that slice 1's own acceptance check is the regression guard for the fan-out half: q01 counts orders off the same stage, so a multiplied stage turns q01 red as well as q02. The dropped-row half has no such guard, because the recording contains no order without a customer.

data.deviationReview:
"One open entry: D-0001 (blueprint R2, no cross-dependency; ADR 0002 is its argument). Reviewed against its exit condition and against the register's second test — whether its argument is still being carried on assertion.

EXIT CONDITION — NOT MET, and slice 2 does not move it. The condition is "a second consumer needs isolation: a different shape of the same structure, or a group that must not see part of it. The generator then gains per-group projections over the same bridge." Slice 2's logistics manager wants the same bridge in the same shape and is not forbidden anything the sales director sees. The stated cost — "the first thing to break is a slice needing a measure defined one way for one reader and another way for another" — has not been incurred either: FREIGHT_ORDERS_AMOUNT means one thing to both readers. The entry stays open, and its status column stays 'open'.

BUT ITS REVIEW TRIGGER FIRES. The register's own Review section says an entry "should also be re-read the moment a second consumer appears, not only when isolation is demanded, because by then the shared structure will already have shaped both readers." Slice 2 is that moment: it is the first slice with a second question and therefore, per ADR 0005 ("one question, one slice, one branch, one page") and `.claude/skills/destination/SKILL.md` ("one app, a page per question"), the first with a second reader of `dar__uss`. This is the review the register asked for, and it should be recorded rather than passed over silently.

WHAT ONE n:1 EDGE DEMONSTRATES. D-0001's 'Why' rests on two clauses: (a) "keys inherit along many-to-one relationships" and (b) "measures stay on the stage that owns them", together making the shared structure "additive by construction". Slice 2 discharges (a) and half of (b), and does not touch the other half.

Demonstrated for the first time: that a key can be carried along an n:1 edge onto the many side, and that summing the many side's measure grouped by the one side's attribute is not multiplied. Concretely, ORDER is the many side, CUSTOMER the one side; there is exactly one bridge row per placed order however many orders a customer has, so `sum(_measure__order__freight_orders_amount)` grouped by `customer.customer_country` totals to the same grand total as ungrouped. That is checkable against the real warehouse and slice 2 should add the check. It is a genuine discharge: the walk now has one edge instead of zero, and ADR 0002's "a zero-edge walk is a valid walk" stops being the only case the code has ever run.

NOT demonstrated, and this is the half the fan trap is named for: a measure owned by the ONE side, summed at a grain where that side appears many times. Slice 2 adds no CUSTOMER event and no CUSTOMER measure, so there is nothing on the parent side that could multiply. ADR 0002's own Confirmation section describes the missing test exactly — "a fixture with two parents and three children, where sum(_measure__parent__…) must still be the parent total and not three times it" — and says it "needs two grains… It lands with the second grain". Slice 2 adds a second ENTITY but still only one grain in the bridge: one stage, order/placed. `docs/questions/README.md` agrees and dates it: "Slice 4 is where the shared-bridge deviation (D-0001) stops being carried on assertion — a second grain is the first thing a measure could multiply across", and slice 4's line reads "the fan-out proof: freight sits on the order and must not multiply across its lines." So slice 2 creates the very measure whose non-multiplication is slice 4's proof, one slice before the thing it must not multiply across exists.

One correction to that dating, in slice 2's favour. ADR 0002 says the fan-out test "cannot be yet" because "this slice has one entity" — but the machinery tests use neutral fixtures held as data files (§6, ADR 0001), not the business model, so the true blocker in slice 1 was that the generator had no relationship support at all, not that the business had one entity. The moment slice 2 teaches the generator to walk an edge, the machinery half of the fan-out test becomes writable: extend `tests/fixtures/dab/model.yaml` with a neutral CHILD entity, a neutral n:1 edge and a measure on PARENT, and assert that the child branch of the union emits a typed NULL in the parent's measure column and that the parent's key is inherited onto the child stage. Slice 2 should write it. What still waits for slice 4 is the *data* half — the same property proved against the real warehouse with real rows, which is what "stops being carried on assertion" properly means.

RECOMMENDATION. Keep D-0001 open and leave its four fields unedited — the reasons that made it necessary have not changed. Do three things instead: (1) update the Review paragraph in `docs/deviations.md`, whose current sentence names slice 1 by hand ("which slice 1's single entity does not exercise at all") and will be stale the moment slice 2 lands — replace it with what is now exercised (the walk, key inheritance, additivity of a child-side measure across a parent-side dimension) and what is not (a parent-side measure at a child grain, which is slice 4); (2) write the neutral-fixture fan-out machinery test in slice 2, since it is now writable, so slice 4 inherits only the data half; (3) record in slice 2's ADR that the second consumer has appeared without demanding isolation, because the register asked for that re-read explicitly and an unrecorded review is indistinguishable from one that never happened.

One footnote on attribution: the blog (*the-consumption-layer-generates-itself*) describes the walk as inheriting "the keys and measures of everything you reach", while ADR 0002 says keys inherit and measures do not. These agree in practice — in a USS the measure *column* exists on every stage and is non-null only on the owning one, which is exactly what `_branch` emits — but the ADR's prose reads as a departure from the blog it cites. Worth a clarifying sentence when 0002 is next touched, not a change of behaviour."
data.theJoinOnPaper:
"WHICH STAGE OWNS THE MEASURE. The `order` stage, on the `placed` event. Freight is a NUMBER on ORDER (one charge per order), and `src/adss/uss.py` requires a sum measure to name an attribute of the event's own entity — `_stage_cte` emits `cast(placed."FREIGHT" AS DECIMAL(28, 8)) AS _measure__order__freight_orders_amount` reading `dab."view_ORDER_hist"`. There is no alternative: CUSTOMER has no freight attribute, and a CUSTOMER stage carrying freight would be the fan trap written down as a design. Slice 2 therefore adds no stage — the bridge still has exactly one branch, one row per order whose PLACED_ON is set, and gains one measure column appended after `_measure__order__placed_orders_count`.

WHICH KEY IS INHERITED. `customer_key`, onto the `order` stage, along ORDER_IS_PLACED_BY_CUSTOMER — many orders, one customer, so the edge is many-to-one and the walk may cross it (blog *the-consumption-layer-generates-itself*: "follow any path that never fans out, and inherit everything along it"). Never the reverse: `order_key` must not propagate to a customer stage, and there is no customer stage in slice 2 anyway. The bridge's key columns become (`order_key`, `customer_key`) in that order — model order, which means CUSTOMER must be APPENDED after ORDER in `dab/model.yaml` or the published contract is rearranged rather than extended (ADR 0002, blueprint B7).

Two code facts make this more than a declaration. `entity_keys()` currently scopes key columns to entities that own an event, and `_generate()` scopes peripherals the same way; CUSTOMER owns no event, so as the code stands there would be neither a `customer_key` column nor a `dar__uss.customer` table. Both must become walk-scoped before any of the rest is possible.

THE GENERATOR'S OWN JOIN — the decision below the documented rule. The `placed` CTE must acquire `CUSTOMER_key` from the relationship object. Two properties are required and neither is written down anywhere: (1) the join is LEFT, or an order with no customer disappears from the bridge and its freight leaves the grand total silently; (2) the relationship object must be reduced to one row per ORDER_key — latest `eff_tmstp` — before the join, or the stage multiplies and `sum(freight)` doubles. The pair carries `eff_tmstp` and `ver_tmstp` (spike 2 finding 4), so more than one row per order is a live possibility the moment a customer id changes across two loads. ADR 0002's fan-trap argument is about measures being copied down an edge; it does not cover a key-inheritance join that fans out, which produces the same wrong number by a different route.

THE ANSWER QUERY. Three references, and the joins are decided one at a time:

  FROM dar__uss._bridge AS b
  INNER JOIN dar__uss._calendar AS cal ON b._event_date = cal.date_key
  LEFT JOIN dar__uss.customer AS c ON b.customer_key = c.customer_key
  WHERE b._event = 'placed'
  GROUP BY cal.quarter_label, c.customer_country
  ORDER BY order_quarter, customer_country

`_calendar` — INNER. `_event_date` is the row's own date, non-null by the column contract, and the calendar is generated dense and daily from `min(_event_date)` to `max(_event_date)` over the bridge itself, so every event date has a calendar row by construction. Note this join is on a date, not a key: ADR 0002's INNER/LEFT rule is about keys and does not literally cover it; INNER is right here for the reason just given, not by appeal to that rule.

`customer` — LEFT, and this is the rule going live. `customer_key` is INHERITED on the `order` stage, not the stage's own key, so ADR 0002 and the dar skill both require LEFT. An INNER join would drop every order whose customer key is null and shrink the freight total — the exact "routing a number through the layers changed it" failure the acceptance check exists to catch, arriving through the query rather than the pipeline.

`dar__uss."order"` — not joined at all. The question needs no ORDER attribute: freight is a measure on the bridge, the quarter comes from the calendar, the country comes from CUSTOMER. If a later question needs one, that join is INNER, because `order_key` is the row's own stage key.

WHAT THE LEFT JOIN COSTS AND WHY IT IS STILL RIGHT. In the recording it costs nothing and buys nothing: all 830 order records carry a non-null CustomerId across 89 distinct values, so LEFT and INNER return identical rows and the acceptance check cannot tell them apart. That is the uncomfortable part — slice 2's headline rule is unenforced by slice 2's own data. Three things fix it: a machinery test over a neutral fixture with a dangling child that asserts the generated stage CTE uses a LEFT join; a data check comparing `sum(_measure__order__freight_orders_amount)` over the whole bridge against `sum(freight)` over `das__staged.orders__current WHERE order_date IS NOT NULL`, which catches both a dropped row and a multiplied one independent of any grouping; and a check that the count of bridge rows with a null `customer_key` equals the count of orders whose customer is absent from `customers__current`.

THE CONTROL QUERY MUST MIRROR IT, ONE JOIN AT A TIME.

  FROM das__staged.orders__current AS o
  LEFT JOIN das__staged.customers__current AS c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
  WHERE o.order_date IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY strftime(o.order_date, '%Y') || '-Q' || cast(quarter(o.order_date) AS VARCHAR), c.country

LEFT, for the same reason and stated as the same reason — slice 1's question file set the precedent of writing down that both queries take the same position deliberately rather than by coincidence. `WHERE o.order_date IS NOT NULL` mirrors the stage's own `WHERE placed."PLACED_ON" IS NOT NULL`; without it the control counts freight the bridge cannot hold, and this matters more for a sum than it did for slice 1's count, because a reader may reconcile the total against the source's total freight. The quarter label must be composed to match `_calendar.quarter_label` exactly ('1996-Q3'), which is `strftime('%Y') || '-Q' || quarter()` in the generator.

THE TWO EDGE CASES, AND WHETHER THE QUESTION HAS TO SAY.

An order with no customer — null CustomerId, or a CustomerId absent from the Customers recording. Bridge row exists, freight present, `customer_key` null; LEFT join yields a null country; the freight lands in a null-country group in BOTH queries and they agree. The generator never invents a member (§1.3), so there is no 'Unknown' row and no `coalesce`. THE QUESTION HAS TO SAY — §1.3 puts the choice in the question file explicitly, and slice 1's `## Nulls` section is the precedent. Neither case occurs in the orders recording (zero null CustomerIds in 830 records), and whether any of the 89 customer ids is absent from Customers cannot be known until `adss das record --contract customers` has run — so the question must state the position, and the slice must actually check the dangling case rather than assume it away.

A customer with no orders. Peripheral row exists; no bridge row anywhere, because there is no customer stage and no order points at them. The query drives from `_bridge`, so that customer never appears — and neither does their country, unless another customer in it ordered. Both queries behave identically, so the check stays green. This is correct for the question as asked: no order means no freight, and a zero row would require a RIGHT or FULL join the architecture does not offer and the question does not ask for. NO RULE REQUIRES THE QUESTION TO SAY — this is a consequence of the grain, not a null-handling choice. But one sentence is worth writing anyway, because "why is Poland missing?" is the first thing the logistics manager will ask, and the honest answer is that no customer there has ever ordered."
gaps: The columns of the relationship pair object are unrecorded. Spike 2 counted `ORDER_CUSTOMER_x` at 3 rows and listed it as a BASE TABLE, but never ran DESCRIBE on it and never selected from it. `DESCRIBE dab.view_ORDER_IS_PLACED_BY_CUSTOMER` was captured (ORDER_key, CUSTOMER_key, type_key, eff_tmstp, ver_tmstp); the `_x` table's shape was not, and the daana documentation in the blog folder never describes it either. ADR 0002 instructs the generator to read this object, so the record depends on a shape nobody has looked at.

ADR 0002's reason for rejecting the relationship VIEW is not backed by any spike observation. The record says those views "rank pairs by effective timestamp and keep the open rows, [so] a changed foreign key can drop out of the view entirely". No spike captured the view's SQL definition, and no spike changed a foreign key across two loads. This is the argument that decides which DAB object the generator reads, and it is currently reasoned rather than observed.

No relationship has ever been observed loading under the configuration this repository mandates. Spike 2's ORDER mapping used `ingestion_strategy: TRANSACTIONAL` with `batch_expression: ingested_at` and `entity_effective_timestamp_expression: order_date` — both forbidden here by M3 and M4. So the only evidence that `ORDER_CUSTOMER_x` is populated at all comes from a configuration conventions §1.4 refuses. Whether the pair object is produced correctly under `FULL_LOG` + `extracted_at` is untested by anything.

What the engine does with a null or dangling foreign key is unknown. Does `target_transformation_expression: customer_id` evaluating to NULL produce no pair row, or a pair row with a null CUSTOMER_key? Does a customer id that exists on the order but in no customer record produce a pair row pointing at a CUSTOMER_key that has no `_desc` rows? Neither was exercised — spike 2's three orders all had valid customers. Both cases change what the bridge holds.

Whether daana's model-level relationship block accepts an `id` key is unknown. The documented shape (blog `doc-ch1.txt`) is `name: IS_PLACED_BY` with `source_entity_id` and `target_entity_id` and no `id`, but conventions §1.2 requires that "entity, attribute and relationship identifiers are UPPER_SNAKE_CASE, with `id` and `name` holding the identical string". If the schema has no `id` key for a relationship, that clause cannot be satisfied and needs clarifying; if it does, nothing has confirmed it.

Nothing establishes how many customers Northwind has or whether any has no orders. 89 distinct CustomerIds appear across the 830 recorded orders; the Customers recording does not exist yet. Whether the 89 are a strict subset of the customers, and whether any recorded customer id on an order is absent from Customers, are both determinable only after `adss das record --contract customers` runs — and both change what the question's null section has to say.

No rule exists for the generator's own inheritance join. Conventions and ADR 0002 state the INNER/LEFT rule for the *reader's* query only. That the stage's join to the relationship object must be LEFT, and must be reduced to one row per source key before joining, is nowhere written — and both failures are silent (a shrunk total, a doubled total).

No rule forbids an answer query joining one peripheral to another. `check_question` only checks which schemas are named, so slice 2 could be faked entirely — model an ORDER foreign-key attribute, join `dar__uss."order"` to `dar__uss.customer` on it, and never touch the inherited key — while every test and check stays green.

No rule says how a NUMBER attribute in `model.yaml` is named relative to the §2 measure that sums it, nor how their two definitions divide the labour. §2 governs measure ids in `uss.yaml`; §1.2 governs attribute ids in `model.yaml`; nothing connects them, and the first sum makes them adjacent.

No rule says what `effective_timestamp:` should be for a new attribute. `src/adss/model.py` does not read the key at all — it is engine-only configuration — and neither conventions nor the dab skill mentions it, yet slice 2 adds several attributes and will pick values for all of them silently. The existing model has `false` on ORDER_NUMBER, `true` on DESTINATION_COUNTRY, and nothing on the START_TIMESTAMP; the neutral fixture uses `true` for its NUMBER attribute.

Nothing says where the DOUBLE cast for charting belongs. The destination skill says to cast aggregates to DOUBLE; ADR 0005 says the page runs `uss.sql` verbatim; `checks.py` compares result tuples with `==`. Put the cast in the query and the first sum measure fails the acceptance check on float-versus-Decimal comparison, with numbers that print identically.

Nothing says what `answer.png` is when one app renders two questions. `docs/questions/01-.../answer.png` is byte-identical to `.screenshots/app.png`, `Project.destination` is a single hardcoded file, and `shoot()` writes one image at a fixed 1800px height. A second question makes the page taller (truncation risk) and makes one screenshot the record for two questions — while ADR 0005 says the picture records what *that* question was accepted on. Whether q01's accepted image is left alone (it should be) and how q02's is produced are both undecided.

The measure has no currency and nothing says what to do about it. Northwind's Freight carries no currency property, and the engine's type vocabulary has a `UNIT` type for exactly this (daana's own example pairs `order_value_amount` with `order_value_currency`). S1 forbids inventing one in DAS. So the honest move is a definition that records the absence — but no rule says a money measure must state its currency or say that the source does not, and §2's unit slot (`amount`) does not carry it.
